(iv) NaOH is a strong alkali: it is corrosive and would damage body tissues; also difficult to store (absorbs CO2/water).

(Q8(d) on the paper.) Compare the anions formed:

In the alkoxide RO− the negative charge is localised on one O atom, giving high charge density that strongly attracts H+ back, so propan-1-ol does not ionise.

In the carboxylate ion RCOO− the charge is delocalised over the C and both O atoms (resonance), lowering the charge density, so the ion is stable and H+ is released.

Alternative: the electronegative C=O oxygen withdraws electrons from the C, which in turn withdraws from the O–H oxygen, weakening the O–H bond.

Water is both acidic and basic (amphiprotic): one H2O molecule acts as an acid by donating H+ (becoming OH−), the other as a base by accepting H+ (becoming H3O+):
H2O + H2O ⇌ H3O+ + OH−
O2− (oxide ion): the conjugate base is what remains after OH− loses a proton.

Compare with equal concentrations (0.10 mol dm−3), either:

  • Electrical conductivity: strong acid is a good conductor, weak acid a poor conductor (fewer ions); or
  • pH meter (or universal indicator): strong acid has lower pH (≈1), weak acid higher pH (≈3).

Litmus is not acceptable (it only shows acid/base). Reaction rate with Mg/CaCO3 is also a valid method.

(iii) HIn ⇌ H+ + In−, where HIn (a weak acid) and In− have different colours. In acid, excess H+ shifts equilibrium left → colour of HIn. In base, OH− removes H+, shifting equilibrium right → colour of In−.

(iv) Ka = [H+][In−]/[HIn]. At the colour change [HIn] = [In−], so Ka = [H+] and pKa = pH of the end point.

(v) The equivalence point is at pH ≈ 8–9, so choose an indicator with pKa ≈ 8–9 (e.g. phenolphthalein).

Sodium ethanoate: Na+ (from a strong base) does not react with water, but CH3COO− (conjugate base of a weak acid) does: CH3COO− + H2O ⇌ CH3COOH + OH−, so the solution is basic.

Ammonium ethanoate: NH4+ is a weak acid (NH4+ ⇌ NH3 + H+) and CH3COO− a weak base of similar strength (Ka ≈ Kb), so the H+ and OH− produced roughly balance → approximately neutral.

SO42− is the conjugate base of a strong acid, so it has no effect on pH.

Al3+ (as [Al(H2O)6]3+) is acidic because the small, highly charged ion polarises its water ligands: [Al(H2O)6]3+ ⇌ [Al(H2O)5(OH)]2+ + H+

The H+ neutralises OH− in the basic pool water, lowering the pH.

For an –OH to be acidic the O–H bond must break, releasing H+.

  • In –COOH the second (C=O) oxygen withdraws electron density from the O–H bond, weakening it and making H+ loss easier.
  • The carboxylate ion formed, –COO−, is stabilised by delocalisation of the negative charge over both O atoms.

The alcohol –OH has neither effect, so it is not acidic.

Brønsted–Lowry: acid = proton (H⁺) donor; base = proton acceptor. e.g. HNO3 (acid) + H2O (base) → H3O⁺ + NO3⁻.

Lewis: acid = electron-pair acceptor; base = electron-pair donor. e.g. BF3 (acid) + NH3 (base) → F3B–NH3, or Cu²⁺ (acid) + 4NH3 (base) → [Cu(NH3)4]²⁺.

The acid and base must be identified on the left-hand side. The bond formed in a Lewis reaction is a dative covalent (coordination) bond: both electrons come from the base.

A strong acid is completely dissociated (ionized) in water; a weak acid is only partially dissociated.

Examples: strong – HCl, HNO3, H2SO4; weak – CH3COOH, H2CO3.

• An indicator is a weak acid (or base): HIn ⇌ H⁺ + In⁻.
  • HIn and In⁻ have different colours.
  • Adding acid (H⁺) shifts the equilibrium to the left → colour of HIn.
  • Adding alkali (OH⁻ removes H⁺) shifts it to the right → colour of In⁻.

(ii) NH3 added to HCl (strong acid–weak base): starts at pH ≈ 1 (same as given graph); the vertical section lies mostly in the acidic region (equivalence pH ≈ 5); levels off around pH 9–10. Indicator: methyl orange (or methyl red, bromophenol blue, bromocresol green).

(i) Kw = [H+][OH−] (or [H3O+][OH−]) – square brackets required.

(ii) Water is always in equilibrium with H+ and OH−, and [OH−] = Kw/[H+]; however large [H+] is, [OH−] is small but never zero.

(iii) Ionization of water is endothermic, so increasing temperature shifts the equilibrium to the right (to absorb the added heat); [H+] and [OH−] both increase, so Kw increases.

(iv) pH decreases (below 7) because [H+] increases and pH = −log[H+]. The water is still neutral since [H+] = [OH−] ("more acidic" is not accepted).

(ii) e.g. sulfurous acid, H2SO3 (or HNO2 or H2CO3). Effects: corrodes marble/limestone buildings and statues, leaches nutrients from soils, damages plants, or acidifies lakes. Naming an oxide (e.g. SO2) is not accepted.

(ii) Fe3+ has a small radius and high charge (high charge density). It polarizes the O–H bonds of its water ligands, which then release H+: [Fe(H2O)6]3+ ⇌ [Fe(H2O)5(OH)]2+ + H+.
